title: Firmware Unlock Doubles Tensor Throughput Tests Monetization
takeaways: The firmware update removes the half‑speed AI throttle on RTX 4090 and other RTX 20‑40 series GPUs, delivering a 2× boost in peak tensor throughput and cutting typical generative‑AI training time by about 50% without additional hardware.

Nvidia’s Vera Rubin chips are expected to generate $40 billion of revenue per gigawatt, supporting a FY2028 revenue growth target of roughly 70% and a year‑over‑year gross‑margin rise of 255 basis points to 62%.
Operating margin expanded by 64 basis points quarter‑over‑quarter as costs grew 19 percentage points slower than revenue year‑over‑year, a cost‑revenue gap also seen at Micron and Alphabet.
script:
This is Account Signals. Today, NVIDIA.

The quarter was reported on August 26, 2026, and the headlines still shape the conversations you’ll have with customers this week.

Tom’s Hardware reported a firmware exploit that removes a half‑speed AI throttle on RTX 4090, doubling its peak tensor rate.

Doubling tensor throughput sounds huge—how does that change the compute budget for a typical generative‑AI workload?

Unlocking the full silicon speed lets customers finish training runs in roughly half the time or run inference at twice the token rate without buying extra GPUs.

Is the fix something you can push out to existing hardware, or does it require new silicon?

It’s a firmware update, so it can be rolled out to any RTX 20, 30 or 40‑series board that already ships with the throttle.

That means a quick win for enterprises that already own those GPUs and are feeling the pinch of AI‑heavy workloads.

The Motley Fool quoted Jensen Huang saying Vera Rubin chips will generate $40 billion in revenue per gigawatt.

What does $40 billion per gigawatt tell us about Nvidia’s growth runway?

Higher revenue per power unit means each megawatt of compute delivers more cash, supporting the company’s guidance for roughly 70 percent revenue growth in fiscal 2028.

How does that revenue density translate into the margins we see in the filing?

Operating margin expanded by 64 basis points quarter‑over‑quarter, reflecting the higher mix of premium AI compute that carries a larger profit cushion.

What’s driving that operating margin expansion beyond the product mix?

Costs grew slower than revenue by 19 percentage points year‑over‑year, widening the margin gap and allowing operating profit to climb faster than top‑line growth.

Is that cost discipline unique to Nvidia, or are we seeing a broader trend?

The same direction—costs grew slower than revenue—is also currently true at Micron and Alphabet.

Given the supply‑constrained outlook, can Nvidia keep that cost advantage without sacrificing growth?

Management says the supply bottleneck is temporary, and the higher‑margin AI stack—hardware, software and services—should keep the cost‑to‑revenue ratio favorable.

Gross margin expanded by 4 basis points quarter‑over‑quarter; can you explain what gross margin actually measures?

Gross margin is the share of each sales dollar left after the cost of building the product, so a 4‑basis‑point rise signals a slight improvement in production efficiency or pricing power.

And the year‑over‑year expansion of 255 basis points—does that reflect the same dynamics?

Yes, the year‑over‑year lift shows that over the past year Nvidia has moved further up the value chain, capturing more profit per unit sold.

Net margin sits at 62 percent—how does that compare to operating margin?

Net margin includes all items after operating profit; it’s slightly lower than operating margin but still strong, indicating limited non‑operating drag.

The filing notes net income grew faster than operating income by 1.8 percentage points year‑over‑year—what’s behind that?

That gap suggests favorable non‑operating factors, such as tax benefits or share‑repurchase gains, adding to the bottom line beyond core operations.

Revenue growth is accelerating, with the year‑over‑year growth rate 20.6 percentage points higher than last quarter—what’s fueling that acceleration?

AI demand is outpacing supply, with hyperscalers adding 2 million GPUs through AWS and a $2 trillion industry backlog driving sequential revenue lifts.

How does the broader financing environment affect those capital‑intensive AI projects?

The 10‑year Treasury yield is 5.0 percent.

It is up 0.31 percentage points from three months ago, raising the cost of capital for large‑scale data‑center builds.

The 10‑year minus 2‑year spread sits at 0.32 percentage points.

It is down 0.03 percentage points, indicating a flattening yield curve that can ease long‑term financing for hyperscalers.

Jensen Huang reaffirmed a $4 trillion AI‑spending projection—does that hold up given the higher financing costs?

Huang’s confidence rests on the expanding AI stack and the higher revenue per gigawatt, which together keep demand robust even as borrowing costs rise.

Tom’s Hardware also reported Nvidia is discussing a $2,000‑per‑GPU annual software fee for agents on AI factories—how does that fit into the revenue picture?

That fee, if adopted broadly, would add a recurring software stream on top of hardware sales, boosting per‑GPU revenue without extra silicon cost.

Would customers see that as a cost increase or as value‑added automation?

If the software delivers measurable efficiency gains, customers may view it as a net cost saving, especially when it replaces manual orchestration of AI pipelines.

MarketWatch ran a headline that Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom could buy Meta shares as part of a $35 billion stock offering—what strategic purpose could that serve?

Participating would give Nvidia a strategic foothold in Meta’s AI ecosystem, potentially aligning future workloads with Nvidia’s hardware.

Yahoo Finance noted the closing price was $216.02.

The modest price gain shows the market’s positive reaction to recent growth cues while still pricing in supply constraints.

The NVIDIA Developer blog announced Mission Control 2.5, which adds autonomous recovery to Kubernetes clusters, reducing downtime for AI workloads.

The same blog highlighted Minerva, a system that turns telemetry chaos into peak GPU yield, improving overall efficiency.

Motley Fool ran a headline that Elon Musk and SpaceX delivered incredible news to Nvidia that could help the stock double in the next year.

Yahoo Finance noted Anthropic makes more per employee than every Magnificent Seven company but Nvidia.

A headline from yahoo_finance compared flat revenue trends at Intel with rapid expansion at Nvidia.

The Motley Fool warned that not Nvidia, this chip stock has more upside, according to Wall Street.

Arista Networks is winning AI data center network share, according to yahoo_finance.

With all these developments, what two high‑leverage questions should I ask Jensen Huang today?

First, ask how Nvidia plans to monetize the firmware unlock across its installed base while protecting revenue from future hardware upgrades, given the $2,000‑per‑GPU software fee as a reference point.

Second, probe the timeline and scale of Vera Rubin production ramp, linking it to the $40 billion per gigawatt revenue target and the 70 percent fiscal‑2028 growth guidance.

Those questions tie directly to the margin expansions and cost‑revenue dynamics we’ve discussed, giving me solid footing.

Finally, consider asking where Nvidia sees the biggest risk to sustaining its cost‑growth advantage, especially as the 10‑year yield climbs and supply constraints linger.

If that risk materializes, it could pressure the operating margin expansion we’re counting on.

Exactly, and it would also test the assumption that revenue per gigawatt can keep rising as hardware scales.

So the open question is whether Nvidia can keep the cost‑revenue gap widening while the macro environment tightens.

That’s the strategic tension you’ll need to surface in your next conversation.
